summary: This Standards Track document defines new IPFIX Information Elements for exporting on-path delay. The delay is measured between the node that adds an OAM header and each transit or decapsulating node that handles it, as computed by an on-path telemetry protocol. IPFIX can then carry those measurements to collectors.

plainLanguage.summary: A package's trip is timed at each stop. This gives a standard way to write down those times and send them to the person who is watching.

questions: how to export on-path delay in ipfix
subtitle: Four new IPFIX Information Elements for exporting per-node on-path delay measured by telemetry in packet headers.

tldr.problem: Operators want to see where delay builds up for specific customer traffic, which means reporting delay metrics from network devices in the context of the data plane. IPFIX had no standard way to export on-path delay measured between an OAM encapsulating node and each node after it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four IPFIX Information Elements, for the mean, minimum, maximum and sum of on-path delay in microseconds, and registers matching entries in the IANA Performance Metrics Registry. Nodes compute delay from a timestamp added by the OAM header encapsulating node and export it in Flow Records.
tldr.outcome: Collectors can see which node, interface or next hop adds how much delay, with less export bandwidth than exporting every packet. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9951 is a Standards Track document published in April 2026 with the status Proposed Standard, and it is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It defines the four path-delay Information Elements for IPFIX.

sections.title: Reporting Delay with IPFIX
sections.content:
Network operators keep statistical views of delay to find where, how much and why delay is abnormal for specific customers or services. For that, delay metrics need to be reported from both data and control planes, and in the context of customer data-plane traffic. That also reveals changes in forwarding paths, such as new intermediate hops or interfaces, and how they affect delay.

Delay is measured with an On-Path Telemetry protocol, which inserts metadata, including a timestamp reference, into the packet when it enters the monitored domain. Examples named in the RFC are IOAM (RFC 9197) and Enhanced Alternate Marking.

Two modes are recognized. In passport mode only the decapsulating node reports. In postcard mode transit nodes also export data. This document is primarily applicable to postcard mode and defines four new IPFIX Information Elements, as specified in RFC 7011.
sections.plainLanguage: Network owners want to know which part of the road makes a delivery slow. This gives every stop a standard way to report how long the trip has taken so far.

sections.title: The Three Kinds of Node
sections.content:
The RFC defines three roles for nodes in the monitored OAM domain.

  • The OAM header encapsulating node receives IP packets, adds an OAM header and writes the timestamp into it.
  • An OAM header transit node measures the delay between the timestamp in the packet and the time the packet arrived.
  • The OAM header decapsulating node does the same measurement and then removes the OAM header.

In the RFC's example, the encapsulating node is R0, transit nodes are R1 and R2, and the decapsulating node is R3. R1 exports delay D1, R2 exports D2, and R3 exports the total delay D3 for the same flow.
sections.plainLanguage: One person stamps the start time on the package. Everyone along the route checks their clock against the stamp. The last person also takes the stamp off.

sections.title: Four New Information Elements
sections.content:
The delay is the difference between the timestamp inserted into the packet at the encapsulating node and the time recorded at the transit or decapsulating node, assuming the devices have synchronized time. The four elements export the mean, the lowest, the highest and the sum of the measured path delay for the packets of a Flow.

Each element is in microseconds, uses the data semantics deltaCounter, and is linked to a registered performance metric. The mean, minimum and maximum are unsigned32, while the sum is unsigned64. Because these are performance metrics, they are also registered in the IANA Performance Metrics Registry under RFC 8911, with names such as OWDelay_HybridType1_IP_RFC9951_Seconds_Mean. The mean, minimum, maximum and sum are computed over packets with a finite one-way delay; undefined delays are excluded.
sections.plainLanguage: For all the packages in one group, a stop can report the fastest trip, the slowest trip, the average trip, or the total time added up.

sections.title: Mean Versus Sum
sections.content:
Computing delay on the transit and decapsulating nodes lets the Flow Record aggregate it, which reduces both export bandwidth and Collector processing. The cost is that the Exporter's Metering Process must cache and process each packet, especially to compute a mean under Flow Aggregation (RFC 7015).

A cheaper option is to export the sum of delays and let the Collector divide by the packet count. The mean can be calculated by dividing pathDelaySumDeltaMicroseconds by packetDeltaCount at collection time.

If nodes did no delay processing at all, each packet would have to be exported as its own Flow Record with timestamps, and the Collector would have to compute the delay metrics and rebuild the aggregated record.
sections.plainLanguage: Either each stop does the averaging itself, which takes effort, or it hands over the total and the number of packages and lets the receiver do the division.

sections.title: Use Cases and Encoding Examples
sections.content:
Aggregating the delay across IPFIX dimensions answers operational questions. With node ID and egress interface, it shows which interface adds how much delay. With next-hop address, MPLS top label or the SRv6 active segment, it shows which forwarding path adds delay. With BGP community lists, it shows which group of prefixes accumulates delay at which node. With addresses, ports and protocol, it shows path delay from a source to a specific application.

The RFC's example table shows delays that grow along the path, for example 22 microseconds at R1, 42 at R2 and 122 at R3. The appendix gives two IPFIX encodings for one aggregated flow of 5 packets: one exports the mean (36 microseconds) with minimum 22 and maximum 74, and the other exports the sum (180 microseconds) instead of the mean. Template IDs 256 and 257 are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Because every stop reports its own time, you can find out which stop is slow, like finding the traffic jam on a map of the road.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Delay numbers are only meaningful if clocks agree. The RFC says clock synchronization between the nodes is needed, that NTP can be used, and that the clock-precision recommendation in RFC 5153 for IPFIX applies.

The sum is unsigned64 to handle large delays and many packets. As an example, a Flow Record with a path delay of 100 milliseconds cannot observe more than 42949 packets without overflowing an unsigned32 counter. Reduced-size encoding from RFC 7011 may be used when 32 bits is enough.

Delay is computed over the Flow Record's lifetime, so a long-running flow can hide when the delay happened. A smaller expiration timeout in the Metering Process can help. Implementations should also document where in the forwarding plane the timestamp is introduced, for example at receive or at transmit time.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone's clocks must show the same time, or the trip times will be wrong. And one long summary can hide the slow moment, so you can ask for shorter summaries.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered four Information Elements in the IPFIX Information Elements registry: pathDelayMeanDeltaMicroseconds (530), pathDelayMinDeltaMicroseconds (531), pathDelayMaxDeltaMicroseconds (532) and pathDelaySumDeltaMicroseconds (533). It also added four metrics to the Performance Metrics Registry, with identifiers 27, 28, 29 and 30 for the mean, minimum, maximum and sum.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list now has four new entries with their own numbers, so everyone uses the same names for these measurements.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new elements do not directly introduce security issues, but delay metrics may be sensitive for privacy or business reasons. Exporting them may also make attacks possible by the receiver of the information that would otherwise be possible only for direct observers of the flow.

IPFIX collectors MUST ensure that data comes from trusted sources, since accepting data from unauthenticated sources could lead to spoofing, policy misapplication or denial of service. The protocol carrying the data must protect integrity and confidentiality, as covered by the IPFIX security considerations in RFC 7011.
sections.plainLanguage: Delay reports can show where a network is weak, so only trusted people should get them, and the receiver should only listen to trusted reporters.

viz.caption: THE FOUR NEW IPFIX INFORMATION ELEMENTS

items.label: pathDelayMeanDeltaMicroseconds
items.desc: Mean path delay of all packets in the Flow, unsigned32.

items.label: pathDelayMinDeltaMicroseconds
items.desc: Lowest path delay of all packets in the Flow, unsigned32.

items.label: pathDelayMaxDeltaMicroseconds
items.desc: Highest path delay of all packets in the Flow, unsigned32.

items.label: pathDelaySumDeltaMicroseconds
items.desc: Sum of path delay of all packets in the Flow, unsigned64.
